text:
Australia's richest woman Gina Rinehart has called for special economic zones to help develop northern Australian resource projects, with companies given permission to employ cheap overseas labour.

Ms Rinehart put forward the idea, which would also include major tax breaks for mine construction firms, because she fears Australia risks losing its key Chinese export market to  more competitive African resources developments.

In an open letter to  The West Australian , Ms Rinehart says Rio Tinto's decision to team up with Chinese investors to develop its massive low-cost iron ore deposit in the Simandou province of Guinea could undermine WA's lucrative but higher-cost Pilbara mines.

"Simandou is a very high-grade iron ore province that, when developed, will be able to produce not only iron ore for decades at low cost, but once infrastructure is established, will pave the way for other minerals in  serious competition to Australia's interests," she said.

"Rio is wanting to take advantage of Guinea's relatively low labour costs to export iron ore in increasing quantities to Asian markets."

Just over a year ago, Ms Rinehart finally achieved her father Lang Hancock's long-held dream of establishing an iron ore mine with the development of the Hope Downs project - in partnership with Rio.

Ms Rinehart said that the threat to Australia's competitiveness "could not be ignored" and proposed the Commonwealth grant concessions over an undisclosed area in the north of the country in order to encourage major project investment to remain in Australia which would then generate Government revenue. These concessions would include tax breaks for infrastructure firms and changes to Australia's immigration laws to let in cheaper offshore workers to help get projects off the ground.

"We should allow competitive and temporary short-term workers to build our projects, say for a duration of up to two years  or so," she said.

Current laws require that temporary overseas workers who are employed on 457 visas  be given the same conditions as Australians.  AMWU secretary Steve McCartney said that the idea was "rubbish" and that higher wage costs had not stopped the massive $43 billion Gorgon gas project from going ahead.

"Gina is trying to create something that isn't there and push wages and conditions down so that firms can make higher profits," he said.
